INTRO (before the video starts)
Welcome back to Let Me Address This TV. It's
your man Showtime, and today — oh, today we
got a FIGHT. Jubilee sat ONE trans woman
down in a circle with TWENTY trans
activists, and told everybody: defend your
position. Blaire White — conservative,
trans, and she did NOT come to make friends.
Her first claim? Trans women should NOT
compete in women's sports. Twenty people who
disagree with everything she stands for, one
chair, and a red flag system where the room
can vote you out when they're tired of you.
Two million people have watched this in five
days and the comments are a WAR. So we're
gonna watch the three biggest claims —
sports, kids and medical transition, and the
locker room fight that broke the internet —
and I'm gonna tell you who actually won.
Let's get into it.
BEAT 1 — Claim 1: Sports (cut 0:00–24:06)
[Watch the Blossom exchange fully, then
pause after the "evidence" fight]
Stop right there. Did y'all catch that?
Blaire came with studies — printed out, in
her hand — and the answer she kept getting
was 'I need data.' She GOT data in her lap!
Now look, I'm not saying every number she
quotes is gospel, but in a DEBATE, the
person asking for receipts can't refuse to
read the receipts when they show up. That's
round one energy right there.
[After the NCAA "less than 10 athletes"
exchange, ~cut 21:00]
Now THAT was a point for the room. Less than
ten trans athletes in the whole NCAA —
Blaire's answer is 'sports is bigger than
college,' and she's right that it is, but if
we're keeping score, the room landed that
one. Write it down: room 1, Blaire 1. This
is a real fight, that's why two million
people watched it.
[After the claim closes]
Claim one is in the books. And notice —
nobody got voted out for being boring. Every
single person in that chair came with smoke.
Claim two is where it gets PERSONAL. Medical
transition for minors. Watch what happens
when the person sitting across from Blaire…
is living proof of her argument.
BEAT 2 — Claim 2: Minors & medical
transition (cut 24:06–43:20)
[After Maebe's puberty-blocker defense]
So Maebe's argument is: blockers are
reversible, they're a pause button. Blaire's
argument is the Cass Review — the biggest
review ever done on this — said the evidence
is WEAK. Two people, two completely
different relationships with the word
'evidence.' Y'all tell me in the comments
which standard we're using, because we can't
use both.
[The detransitioner exchange, cut ~34:00 —
let it play COMPLETELY, then:]
…Wow. Did y'all just see what I saw? Blaire
tells the room most kids with gender
dysphoria grow out of it if you leave them
alone — and the person arguing with her says
'that didn't happen to me'… while sitting
there NOT on hormones, NOT identifying as
trans anymore. The host had to step in
because the room felt it. She proved
Blaire's point BY ACCIDENT, in real time, on
camera. That's the moment this whole video
is gonna be remembered for. I don't care
what side you're on — that's incredible
television and an incredible argument
moment.
[Claim close]
Two claims down. Now the one that produced
the clip your cousin already sent you.
Locker rooms. Predatory behavior. And a
nineteen-year-old who says the words 'it's
just a penis' to a room full of adults. Roll
it.
BEAT 3 — Claim 4: Predatory behavior &
locker rooms (cut 43:20–70:00)
[After "I'm a trans woman, I'm MALE," cut
THAT'S the line. A trans woman, on Jubilee,
telling twenty activists 'trans women are
MALE, I am male' — and meaning it as a
BIOLOGY statement, not an identity one. Half
the room's whole argument depends on NOT
saying that sentence. She just said it in
the first three minutes of the claim. Watch
their faces.
[Locker-room exchange, cut ~64:19 — let it
play COMPLETELY, then:]
'It's just a penis.' 'NO ONE IS TALKING
ABOUT YOUR GRANDMA!' [laugh] Y'all. Y'all.
The activist's argument is 'it doesn't
bother ME' — Blaire's argument is 'you don't
get to decide what every woman in that
locker room has to accept.' That's the whole
debate in one exchange: is the standard the
person who's comfortable, or the person who
ISN'T? Put your answer in the comments, and
be honest, because your daughter, your mama,
your grandma uses that locker room too.
[Final moments]
And that is how it ends. Twenty activists,
one Blaire, and I gotta keep it a buck with
y'all…
OUTRO / CTA
My verdict: Blaire White won the sports
claim on evidence, she won the minors claim
on that detransitioner moment, and the
locker room claim wasn't even close. The
room's best moment was the NCAA numbers in
claim one — credit where it's due. But
overall? She walked into a 20-on-1 and
walked out with the two most viral clips of
the week. THAT'S a win. Now I need YOUR
verdict — the poll is up on the Community
tab: Should trans women compete in women's
sports? Yes, no, separate league, or only
after full transition. Vote, then argue
about it in the comments like you mean it.
If you rock with real debates, hit subscribe
— we're on the road to the Partner Program
and every sub counts. It's Showtime, Let Me
Address This TV. I'll see y'all in the next
one.
(read aloud in one pass)
Showtime — this is written to be read
straight through. [PAUSE] marks are where
you stop the video and talk. Everything
else, let it play and react live.
COLD OPEN (before you press play, straight
to camera)
"Hold on, hold on. Before we get into
anything — I need y'all to hear two
questions. Same situation. Same alcohol. Two
different answers… and the answers are gonna
tell you everything about where we are right
now. Watch this."
INTRO (right after your intro sting)
"Welcome back to Let Me Address This TV,
it's your boy Showtime, and today — oh,
today is a good one. This is from It's
Complicated, the street interview series, a
video called Drunk Sex that has been tearing
the internet UP — millions of views, and
it's still going. They went out and asked
women the simplest pair of questions I've
ever heard. Question one: if a girl is super
drunk and a sober guy has sex with her, is
that rape? Everybody says yes. Immediately.
No hesitation. Question two: if your
boyfriend gets super drunk and has sex with
a sober girl — was he raped… or did he
cheat? …Y'all. The way the answer CHANGED.
Same drunk. Same act. But now he's not a
victim — he's a cheater who should've known
better. We're gonna watch the whole thing —
not just the viral clip, the whole
conversation — plus three more interviews
where they keep digging: what is consent,
should we believe all women, and that 'not
all men' phrase. By the end, YOU tell ME: is
this a double standard, or is there
something I'm missing? Let's get into it."
SEGMENT 1 — DRUNK SEX (cut 00:00–17:24)
Opening beat (first interview, the cold
open): "First thing out the gate — did y'all
hear what she just said? The laws give women
leeway to LIE about this. That's one of
THEIR side saying the quiet part out loud.
Remember that, because it frames this whole
video."
Casino beat (~00:22 in the cut): "Now THIS
is a smart question. You lose ten thousand
dollars in a casino drunk — can you withdraw
consent and get your money back? Everybody
knows that's YOUR responsibility. So why is
sex the only place consent can be withdrawn
AFTER the fact? Watch how they wrestle with
that one."
[PAUSE — THE VIRAL EXCHANGE, cut ~05:33]
"STOP. Stop the video. This is the clip that
broke the internet, so let's do it slow.
Teal hair — question one: super drunk girl,
sober guy. 'YES. That's rape.' Not a blink.
Now flip it. Her boyfriend, super drunk,
sober girl — was he raped or did he cheat?
…'He CHEATED. He's NOT a victim. Why are you
drunk in public? You should be drunk with
me.' MA'AM. If he can't consent, he can't
cheat! Cheating is a CHOICE. You just told
me five seconds ago a drunk person can't
make that choice! Which is it?!"
[PAUSE — braids woman, cut ~05:50–06:19]
"And then Strip girl takes it FURTHER. 'He
bought all five of those drinks, he KNEW he
was gonna get tore up, he was trying to do
the do — he didn't get raped, NO.' So let me
make sure I understand the rule: when SHE
drinks five drinks, she's a victim who
couldn't consent. When HE drinks five
drinks, he's a man with a PLAN. The drinks
are evidence FOR her and AGAINST him. Same
five drinks! …Vegas, y'all. This is right
here on the Strip, Caesars right behind her.
This is my city producing this logic."
Both-drunk beat (~10:00 in the cut): "Now
they ask the question that breaks the whole
thing: what if BOTH of them are drunk? One
of 'em actually says it — 'both graped.'
See, when you follow the logic all the way
down, even THEY land on equal. It's only
when it's him alone that the word changes."
Laws beat (~11:17 in the cut): "Listen to
this part — 'certain laws are targeted
towards men.' That's not me saying it.
That's them. On camera."
Segment closer: "That's part one. And notice
— nobody in that whole segment could keep
the rule the same for both sides for more
than one question. But maybe I'm being
unfair. Maybe when they really sit down and
define consent, it evens out. Let's find out
— this next one is called What Is Consent."
TRANSITION INTO SEGMENT 2
"Same channel, same streets. Now they gotta
define the word itself. Because everything
in part one hangs on one word — consent.
What is it? When can you take it back? And
does the rule move depending on who's
talking?"
SEGMENT 2 — WHAT IS CONSENT? (cut
Opener beat: "First question out the gate is
a trap and they know it — if consent can be
read through body language, why do some
encounters need a safe word? Watch the
wheels turn."
Passive-yes beat: "'Is a passive yes
enough?' Y'all hear how unsure everybody
gets? Because in real life, everybody in
this video has lived the grey area they're
trying to legislate."
Withdrawal beat (mid-segment): [PAUSE]
"Here's the one I need y'all locked in on:
can consent be withdrawn AFTER the fact —
after everything already happened, because
of regret? There's a difference between 'I
was too drunk to agree' and 'I agreed and I
regret it.' One is a crime. The other one is
a bad night. If we erase that line, every
man in America is one regret away from a
charge. And every woman in this video knows
somebody who'd use it — they said so in part
one, the leeway to lie. Connect those dots."
Segment closer: "So consent can be body
language, or NOT body language. It can be
withdrawn, or NOT withdrawn. It depends. And
'it depends' always seems to depend on the
same thing — who's accused and who's
accusing. Which brings us to the slogan.
Should we believe ALL women?"
TRANSITION INTO SEGMENT 3
"They asked it straight: if trust should be
EARNED — and everybody says trust is earned
— then why does 'believe all women' get a
pass? No earning. No evidence. Just believe.
Let's see who defends that and how."
SEGMENT 3 — BELIEVE ALL WOMEN (cut
Opener beat: "Hear that first answer — 'I
would believe MOST women, but…' — that 'but'
is carrying the whole video. Most is not
all. The slogan says ALL."
Victims-vs-narrative beat (~mid-segment):
"This is the real question of the whole
video: are we protecting victims, or are we
protecting a narrative? Because a real
victim deserves to be believed AND a real
accusation deserves evidence. Both things
can be true. The second a system says
'evidence is optional,' it stops protecting
victims and starts handing out weapons — and
part one already showed you women admitting
the weapon gets used."
Due-process beat (~11:00 into the segment):
[PAUSE] "DUE PROCESS. There it is. Somebody
finally said it. That's the whole ballgame —
believe women enough to investigate EVERY
claim seriously, and believe in innocence
enough to prove it before you destroy a man.
That's not anti-woman. That's just… the law
working for everybody. Why is that
controversial?"
Segment closer: "Alright. So the rule bends
on consent, it bends on belief… there's one
phrase left. You've heard it a thousand
times: 'not all men, but always a man.' They
took THAT to the street too. Last one —
let's finish this."
TRANSITION INTO SEGMENT 4
"If men are the problem as a group, what
happens to the men who are victims
themselves? Where do THEY go? That's where
this one starts."
SEGMENT 4 — NOT ALL MEN (cut 47:43–61:25)
Opener beat: "'Not all men, but always a
man.' Okay — but when a man IS the victim,
like the drunk boyfriend in part one… he's a
cheater. When he's not the victim, he's the
suspect. When does a man get to just be a
PERSON in this system?"
Male-victims beat (~mid-segment): [PAUSE]
"Somebody asked it plain: where do male
victims of violence GO? No hotline with his
name on it, no slogan saying believe HIM,
and if he was drunk — y'all already saw it —
he planned it. A man gets hurt and the world
asks what he did to deserve it. A woman gets
hurt and the world asks who did it to her.
THAT. That right there is the whole video in
one sentence."
Closer beat (final answer): "And after all
of that — listen to how it ends. 'Teaching
everybody to do the right thing, no matter
what.' EVERYBODY. Same rules, same
accountability, same protection. That's all
anybody's asking for. Took 'em four videos
to get there, but they got there."
OUTRO / CTA
"So let's tally it up. Drunk girl — victim.
Drunk boyfriend — cheater. Consent —
definable until it isn't. Believe all women
— until due process walks in. Not all men —
but a male victim still can't find the door.
Four interviews, one pattern: the rule is
never the rule. The rule is WHO.
Now I need YOUR verdict, because this is
what we do here. The poll is up on the
Community tab and I want it in the comments
too: if he's drunk — is it rape, or is it
cheating? Pick one and DEFEND it, because I
will be in those comments reading every
single one.
And family — this is not theoretical.
There's a real case, seven young men, the
Cornell 7, where this exact double standard
stopped being a street interview and became
real life. I already broke that whole thing
down — that video is linked right here and
in the pinned comment. Go watch it right
after this.
If you're new here, you know what to do —
hit that subscribe, ring the bell, because
we address it ALL over here, nothing is off
limits. This is Let Me Address This TV, I'm
Showtime… and fellas, apparently you should
only get drunk with your girl. Her words,
not mine. I'm out."
POLL (Community tab, goes up with the video)
"If he's drunk, is it rape or cheating?" —
options: "He was raped — he couldn't
consent" / "He cheated — he's responsible" /
"Depends how drunk he was" / "It's only rape
when it's her"
